opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's something we thought about a lot when we were building the generative agent simulations of a thousand-plus real people.

Surveys are wonderful for what they were designed to do. They're standardized, they're cheap to scale, and because everyone answers the same questions in the same format, you can compare people directly and run clean statistics. If you want to know how attitudes on some policy question are distributed across a population, a well-designed survey is hard to beat. The limitation is that you only learn what you thought to ask. The researcher defines the dimensions up front, so you get a pretty thin slice of a person, a set of points on axes someone else chose.

Interviews are almost the opposite. They're expensive and messy, and harder to analyze in a standardized way, but they let people tell you about themselves in their own terms. You hear the story of where someone grew up, why they changed jobs, how they think about their family, what they worry about. A lot of what actually drives how a person responds to a new situation lives in that context, and it often comes up in ways you never would have anticipated with a fixed questionnaire. A good interviewer can also follow up: "Oh, why do you say that?" That's where a lot of the richness comes from.

What was exciting for us is that language models change the cost-benefit tradeoff. In the past, the reason you couldn't use rich two-hour interviews to make predictions was that it was too hard to turn all that unstructured text into something usable. Now a model can actually take in that whole transcript and reason over it. When we compared agents built from interviews against agents built from just demographics or short persona descriptions, the interview-based agents predicted people's survey responses and behavior much more accurately. In some cases, they came close to how consistently people replicate their own answers two weeks later.

So the way I think about it now is that surveys remain the ruler, the way you measure and evaluate, while interviews are becoming the substrate, the way you actually capture who someone is. Combining the two is where a lot of the power is.

r001.rationale: The response says interviews let people share their stories and personal context, including details that fixed questionnaires may not anticipate, conveying their value for eliciting less predictable information.

r002.rationale: It mentions that interviewers can follow up, but does not describe training an interviewer to maximize insight per unit of interview time.

r003.rationale: It describes surveys as standardized and cheap to scale, but does not identify them as a time-efficient way to collect factual or discrete-choice responses.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, because when we were building the generative agents work and then the thousand-person simulation project, the whole question was really: what is the best input for capturing who a person actually is?

And I think the way I'd frame it is that surveys and interviews are kind of two different instruments with very different trade-offs. Surveys are great at scale and at comparability. If I give the same twenty questions to ten thousand people, I can line everybody up on the same axes, I can run statistics, I can say this population leans this way on this dimension. That's incredibly powerful, and it's why social science has leaned on them for so long. But the weakness is that a survey only ever tells you about the things you already thought to ask. You're imposing a structure on the person before you've met them. And people are weird, in the good sense. The things that make someone distinctive are often the things that don't fit into a Likert scale.

Interviews flip that. A good interview is open-ended, it's generative, it lets the person tell you what matters to them in their own words. You find out that this person's whole political worldview is anchored in something that happened to their family in the eighties, or that their consumption habits come from growing up in a particular small town. You would never have had a checkbox for that. So interviews have this very high information density per person. The cost, obviously, is that they're expensive, they're hard to compare across people, and historically you couldn't do much with that richness computationally.

What's interesting now is that language models actually change the calculus. In our work, we did two-hour interviews with over a thousand people, and we found that feeding those transcripts to a model produced agents that predicted people's own survey responses and experimental behavior substantially better than giving the model their demographics or even a bunch of their survey answers. The interview captured things that the structured data just didn't. So my view has shifted toward thinking the interview is the richer primary source, and the survey is more useful as a way to measure and validate. We used surveys as the ground truth to check whether the interview-based agents were right, which I think is a nice division of labor.

The caveat I'd add is that interviews have their own biases. People present themselves, they narrate, they forget. So I don't think it's interviews versus surveys. I think it's that we finally have tools that can take the messy, qualitative thing seriously, and that opens up a lot.

r001.rationale: The response says open-ended interviews reveal distinctive, unexpected details that would not fit a checkbox or Likert scale.

r002.rationale: It discusses interviews’ richness and cost but does not describe training an interviewer to maximize insight per unit of interview time.

r003.rationale: It describes surveys as scalable and comparable, but does not identify them as time-efficient for collecting factual or discrete-choice responses.

astra-6.text:
I think interviews and surveys have complementary strengths. Surveys let you ask the same questions across a lot of people, so you can compare responses systematically. But you have to decide in advance what to ask and what kinds of answers to make room for. Interviews give you more space to discover what you didn’t know to ask. You can follow up on something surprising and understand the experiences or motivations behind an answer.

So if you want to understand a person, it helps to have both: structured questions that give you comparable measurements, and an open-ended conversation that gives you context for interpreting those measurements.

r001.rationale: It says interviews help uncover things you did not know to ask about and follow up on surprising answers, conveying their value for eliciting less-anticipated information about people.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss training interviewers or maximizing insight per unit of interview time.

r003.rationale: It says surveys can ask the same questions of many people, but does not identify them as time-efficient for collecting factual or discrete-choice responses.

sol-6.1.text:
I think interviews and surveys offer complementary ways of understanding people. Surveys let you ask a consistent set of questions across many people, which is useful for seeing patterns and comparing responses. Interviews give you room to understand the context behind an answer. You can ask, “Why was that important to you?” or “Can you give me an example?” And often that follow-up reveals something you wouldn’t have known to ask about in a survey.

Neither gives you a complete picture of a person. But together, they can help you understand both what people have in common and the experiences and motivations that make their answers different.

r001.rationale: The response says interviews reveal context, motivations, and unexpected follow-up insights, but does not identify them as suited to eliciting long-tail information.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss training an interviewer or maximizing insight per unit of interview time.

r003.rationale: It describes surveys as consistent and useful for comparing many people, but does not characterize them as time-efficient for factual or discrete-choice responses.
